decomposition.reasoning: Classic Latin compound. trans- ("across") is a highly productive prefix in English (transform, transcend, transmit). port- ("carry") from Latin portāre is equally productive (import, export, portable, portal, important). Both morphemes are immediately recognizable to modern learners.

Classic Latin compound: ex- ("out/from") + port- ("carry") = "carry out". Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. ex- appears in export, exclude, exhale, emit; port- appears in transport, import, portable, porter. The decomposition is etymologically accurate and immediately useful to a learner.

From Latin importantem (present participle of importare: "to bring in, to be of consequence"). im- is a variant of in- ("into/toward") + port- ("carry") + -ant (participial/adjectival suffix). The root port- is highly productive in English: transport, export, portable, porter. The prefix im- (in-) also appears widely: import, impose, include. The suffix -ant is common: relevant, significant, dominant.

Classic Latin derivation: port- (carry, from portāre) + -able (capable of being). Both morphemes are fully productive in modern English. port- appears in transport, export, import, report; -able appears in countless words like visible, flexible, readable. The meaning is fully transparent: "capable of being carried."

The word "prognosis" comes directly from Greek prognōsis, composed of the prefix pro- (before/forward) and the root gnos- (know), from gnōsis (knowledge). Both morphemes are productive in English: pro- appears in "predict", "progress", "prologue"; gnos- appears in "diagnosis", "agnostic", "cognition" (Latin cognate), "gnosis". The noun-forming suffix -is is a standard Greek ending visible in "diagnosis", "analysis", "synthesis", etc.

From Greek "diagnosis" = dia- (through/apart) + gnōsis (knowledge/knowing). The root gnos-/gnow- is productive in English: recognize, prognosis, agnostic, cognitive (via Latin cognoscere). The prefix dia- is also productive: diameter, diagonal, dialogue, diagram. The final -e is a silent English back-formation marker from "diagnosis" → "diagnose" (verb), not a meaningful suffix. High confidence.

The word "agnostic" is a well-known Greek compound coined by T.H. Huxley in 1869 from Greek a- (not/without) + gnōsis (knowledge). The root gnos- is productive in English: diagnosis, prognosis, cognition (via Latin cogn-), agnosia. The suffix -tic is a standard Greek adjectival suffix (cf. diagnostic, symbiotic). All three morphemes are recognizable and teach genuine vocabulary connections.

Classic Greek compound: tele- (far) + phon- (sound/voice). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. tele- appears in television, telescope, telepathy, telegram; phon- appears in microphone, phonetics, symphony, saxophone. The trailing -e is a standard anglicisation of the Greek noun ending. Straightforward and unambiguous decomposition.

Two highly productive Greek roots: photo- (light) appears in photosynthesis, photon, photoelectric; graph- (write/record) appears in paragraph, autograph, biography, telegram. Together they literally mean "written/recorded by light" — a perfect description of how early photography worked. Both roots are immediately recognizable and useful to learners.

Classic Greek compound: bio- (life) + connective -o- + log- (study/reason) + -y (noun-forming suffix). Both roots are highly productive in modern English — bio- appears in biography, biosphere, antibiotic; log-/logy appears in geology, psychology, technology. The connective -o- is emitted as a separate morpheme to keep both roots clean and identifiable. Straightforward, unambiguous decomposition.

Two highly productive Greek roots: bio- (life) appears in biology, biosphere, antibiotic, etc.; graph- (write/record) appears in photograph, paragraph, autograph, etc. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. Note: bio- already ends in -o, so no separate connective vowel is needed. Straightforward, unambiguous decomposition.

decomposition.meaning: relating to / having the quality of

decomposition.reasoning: The word "antibiotic" is a transparent Greek compound: anti- (against) + bio- (life) + -tic (adjectival suffix meaning "relating to"). All three morphemes are productive and well-known in English. anti- appears in antisocial, antidote, antifreeze; bio- appears in biology, biography, biosphere; -tic appears in acoustic, magnetic, aquatic. The compound literally means "acting against life" (i.e., against bacterial life). High confidence — clean, well-attested decomposition.

Two highly productive Greek roots: geo- (earth) appears in geology, geopolitics, geometry; graph- (write/describe) appears in photograph, paragraph, biography. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. No connective vowel is needed here as "geo" already ends in -o and "graph" begins with a consonant — the -o is absorbed into the geo- root itself. Standard, well-attested Greek compound.

Classic Greek compound: geo- (earth) + connective vowel -o- + log- (study/reason/word) + noun-forming suffix -y. Both roots are highly productive in English (geo- in geography, geometry, geopolitics; log-/logy in biology, psychology, ecology). Straightforward, high-confidence decomposition.

A classic Greek compound: therm- (heat) + connective vowel -o- + metr- (measure). Both roots are highly productive in modern English. therm- appears in thermal, thermostat, thermos, hypothermia; metr-/meter appears in barometer, speedometer, diameter, geometry. The connective -o- is emitted as a separate morpheme to keep both roots individually visible.

Television is a well-known Greek-Latin hybrid compound. tele- (Greek, "far") is a productive prefix found in telephone, telescope, telepathy. vis- (Latin, "see") is a productive root found in vision, visible, visual, evidence. -ion is a standard Latin nominalising suffix. All three morphemes are highly recognisable and productive in modern English.

Classic Greek compound: micro- (small) + connective vowel -o- + scop- (look/examine). Both roots are highly productive in modern English: micro- appears in microphone, microbe, microchip; scop- appears in telescope, periscope, stethoscope. The decomposition is etymologically sound and immediately useful to a learner.

Two highly productive Greek morphemes: auto- (self) appears in automobile, autonomous, autocrat; graph- (write) appears in photograph, paragraph, biography, telegram. The compound meaning "written by oneself" is transparent and directly useful to a learner.

Classic Greek compound: cardi- (heart, from kardia) + connective vowel -o- + log- (study/reason, from logos) + noun-forming suffix -y. All morphemes are productive in modern English. cardi- appears in cardiac, cardiovascular, electrocardiogram; log-/logy appears in biology, psychology, geology, etc.

Classic Greek compound: derm-/dermat- (skin) + connective vowel -o- + log- (study/reason) + -y (noun-forming suffix). All morphemes are productive in modern English. derm- appears in epidermis, hypodermic; log-/logy appears in biology, geology, psychology. Straightforward and highly learnable.

Classic Greek compound: paed- (child) + connective vowel -o- + iatr- (physician/healing) + adjectival suffix -ic. Both roots are productive in English: paed- appears in pedagogy, paediatrician; iatr- appears in psychiatry, geriatrics. Straightforward and unambiguous decomposition.

Two highly productive Greek roots joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-. dem- (people) appears in epidemic, endemic, demography; crat- (rule/power) appears in aristocrat, autocrat, bureaucrat. The suffix -y nominalises the compound. Decomposition is well-known, unambiguous, and teaches genuinely reusable morphemes.

Two highly productive Greek roots joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-. phil- (love) appears in philanthropy, bibliophile, philharmonic; soph- (wisdom) appears in sophisticated, sophomore. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. Straightforward and uncontroversial decomposition.

Classic Greek compound: phil- (love) + connective -o- + anthrop- (human being) + -y (noun-forming suffix). Both roots are productive and recognizable in modern English vocabulary. phil- appears in philosophy, bibliophile, philharmonic; anthrop- appears in anthropology, misanthropy, anthropomorphic. Clean, unambiguous decomposition.

Straightforward Greek derivation: chron- (time) + -ic (relating to). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. chron- appears in chronology, synchronize, anachronism; -ic appears in historic, democratic, economic. The word literally means "relating to time" — i.e., persisting over a long time. No false-root traps here.

Two productive Greek roots joined by the standard Greek connective vowel -o-. chron- (time) is recognizable in chronic, synchronize, anachronism; log- (study/reason) is recognizable in biology, geology, logic. The -y suffix nominalises the compound. Straightforward and highly learnable decomposition.

A clean, fully transparent Greek compound. syn- (together) is a productive prefix seen in synthesis, symphony, syndrome. chron- (time) is a productive root seen in chronology, anachronism, chronic. -ize is a productive verb-forming suffix seen in modernize, nationalize, etc. All three morphemes are live and learnable.

Hydrogen is a well-established Greek compound: hydr- (water) + connective -o- + gen- (produce/give birth to). The name was coined in the late 18th century because hydrogen produces water when burned. Both roots are productive in modern English: hydr- appears in hydrology, dehydrate, hydraulic; gen- appears in genesis, genetics, oxygen, pathogen. Classic Greek two-root compound with connective vowel -o-.

From French oxygène, coined by Lavoisier from Greek oxys (sharp/acid) + -genes (producing). The name reflects the mistaken 18th-century belief that oxygen was a necessary component of all acids. Both roots are productive in English: oxy- appears in oxide, oxidize, oxymoron; gen- appears in generate, genesis, hydrogen, nitrogen, pathogen.

Greek word directly borrowed into English. The root gen- (birth, origin) is highly productive in English: genetics, generate, pathogen, hydrogen, progenitor, etc. The suffix -esis is a Greek nominalizing suffix meaning "process/act of", also seen in synthesis, hypothesis, parenthesis, diagnosis. Clean, well-known decomposition with strong learner value.

From Latin dictionarium, built on dictio (a saying/word), itself from dicere (to say). The root dict- is highly productive in English (dictate, predict, verdict, diction, contradict). The suffix -ion forms the noun "diction" (manner of speaking), and -ary converts it to an adjective/noun meaning "relating to" or "place for" — as in "a place for words/sayings". All three morphemes are independently recognizable and productive.

Clear Latin compound: pre- ("before") + dict- ("say/tell", from Latin dicere). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. pre- appears in prefix, prepare, prevent, precede, etc. dict- appears in dictate, contradict, verdict, diction, edict, etc. A learner who sees this decomposition gains genuine insight into the word's meaning ("to say beforehand") and can connect it to many other English words.

Straightforward Latin compound: contra- (against) + dict- (say, from dicere). Both morphemes are highly productive in modern English. contra- appears in contrary, contrast, contraband; dict- appears in dictate, predict, verdict, diction. The meaning "speak against" maps directly and transparently onto the word's modern sense.

From Latin veredictum, "truly said" — ver- (true, from verus) + dict- (say, from dicere). Both roots are productive in modern English: ver- appears in verify, verity, veracious; dict- appears in dictate, predict, diction, contradict. No suffix needed — the word itself is a direct borrowing of the Latin past participle form used as a noun.

Manuscript is from Latin manuscriptus, meaning "written by hand" — a clean compound of manus (hand) + scriptus (written, past participle of scribere). Both roots are highly productive in modern English: manu- appears in manual, manufacture, manipulate; script- appears in script, description, prescription, scripture, transcript. No affixes to separate here — the word is a direct Latin compound adopted into English.

The word "description" is a straightforward Latin compound: de- (down/thoroughly) + script- (past participial stem of scrībere, "to write") + -ion (nominalising suffix). All three morphemes are highly productive in modern English. The root scrib-/script- appears in prescribe, subscribe, manuscript, inscription, scripture. The prefix de- appears in descend, define, declare. The suffix -ion appears in action, motion, creation. A textbook decomposition with no false-root traps.

Straightforward Latin decomposition: in- (into/upon) + scrib- (write) + -tion (nominalizing suffix). The root scrib-/script- is highly productive in English (describe, prescribe, manuscript, subscribe). The prefix in- meaning "into/upon" is also productive (insert, inscribe, include). The -tion suffix is one of the most common Latin nominalizing suffixes in English. The whole word literally means "the act of writing into/upon", which matches its real-world meaning (text carved or written on a surface).

Classic Greek compound: psych- (mind/soul) + connective vowel -o- + log- (study/reason) + noun-forming suffix -y. All morphemes are productive in modern English. psych- appears in psychiatry, psychosis, psychic; log-/logy appears in biology, geology, theology. Standard high-confidence decomposition.

The word breaks cleanly into the Latin root mem- (memory/mind) + the noun-forming suffix -or (giving "memoria" in Latin) + the adjectival suffix -ial (relating to). All three morphemes are productive in modern English: mem- appears in memory, remember, commemorate; -or appears in error, horror, honor; -ial appears inorial, remedial, official. The decomposition is etymologically sound and pedagogically useful.

From Latin memoria (memory, recollection), from memor (mindful, remembering). The root mem-/memor- is highly productive in English: remember, memorial, memorize, commemorate, memoir. The -y suffix nominalizes the stem. Clean and unambiguous decomposition.

False-root trap. "Uncle" superficially looks like it could be segmented as "un-" + "-cle", but this is entirely misleading. The word derives from Latin "avunculus" (mother's brother), itself a diminutive of "avus" (grandfather). The word entered English via Old French "oncle". There are no productive English morphemes here — "un-" is not the negating prefix, and "-cle" is not a suffix. Decomposing it would teach the learner a falsehood.

False-root trap. "Island" looks like it could be decomposed as "is-" + "land", but the "s" was never a real morpheme. The word derives from Old English "iegland" (ieg = island/watery land + land), and the "s" was silently inserted in the 16th century through false analogy with the unrelated French/Latin word "isle" (from Latin "insula"). The surface form is etymologically misleading — "is-" is not a prefix and does not carry any meaning. Teaching this as a decomposition would create a false analogy.

False-root trap. "Butter" looks like it could be "butt" + "-er" (as in an agent suffix, "one who butts"), but it is actually borrowed from Greek "boutyron" (βούτυρον) via Latin "butyrum". The "-er" ending is an inseparable part of the borrowed stem, not the Germanic agent suffix. No productive decomposition is possible.

Two productive Greek roots joined by the standard connective vowel -o-. crypt- (hidden) appears in crypt, cryptic, encrypt, apocrypha; graph- (write) appears in photograph, paragraph, autograph, biography. The -y suffix nominalizes the compound. All parts are well-attested and productive in modern English.

Two fully productive Greek roots joined by the standard connective vowel -o-. xen- (stranger/foreigner) appears in xenon, xenophile, xenograft; phob- (fear) appears in phobia, claustrophobia, agoraphobia, hydrophobia. The -ia suffix forms a noun denoting a state or condition, seen in euphoria, insomnia, dystopia. Clean, unambiguous decomposition with no false-root traps.

Clear Latin compound: omni- (all) + vor- (devour/eat) + -e (noun-forming). Both morphemes are productive in English: omni- appears in omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent; -vor- appears in carnivore, herbivore, voracious. Straightforward and high-value for learners.

A clean Latin compound: herba (plant/grass) + connective -i- + vorare (to devour) + nominal -e. Both roots are productive in English: herb- appears in herbal, herbaceous, herbicide; vor- appears in carnivore, omnivore, voracious, devour. This is a textbook case of a learnable decomposition.

Classic Latin compound: carn- (flesh, from caro/carnis) + connective -i- + vor- (devour, from vorare) + noun-forming -e. Both roots are highly productive in English: carn- appears in carnival, carnage, incarnate, reincarnation; vor- appears in herbivore, omnivore, voracious, devour. Straightforward, learner-friendly decomposition.

decomposition.meaning: having the quality of, tending to

decomposition.reasoning: From Latin benevolens (well-wishing): bene- (well/good) + vol- (wish/will, from velle) + -ent (adjectival suffix). All three morphemes are productive and recognizable: bene- appears in benefit, benefactor, benign; vol- appears in voluntary, volunteer, malevolent; -ent appears in confident, dependent, patient. Clean and unambiguous decomposition.

decomposition.meaning: having the quality of, characterized by

decomposition.reasoning: From Latin malevolens: male- (bad/evil, from malus) + vol- (wish/will, from velle) + -ent (adjectival suffix). All three morphemes are productive and recognizable in modern English: male- appears in malfunction, malice, malformed; vol- appears in volunteer, volition, benevolent; -ent appears in dependent, confident, etc. The decomposition is unambiguous and teaches a clear, correct analogy — especially the contrast with "benevolent" (bene- = good + vol- = wish).

From Latin renovare = re- (again) + novare (to make new), from novus (new). All three morphemes are productive in modern English: re- appears in rebuild, reconsider, restore; nov- appears in novel, innovate, novelty; -ate appears in create, activate, generate. Clean, unambiguous Latin formation.
